title: One Siberian lake holds over a fifth of Earth’s fresh surface water
body: Lake Baikal in Siberia is 636 km long and only 79 km wide, yet it holds about 23,600 cubic kilometres of water, roughly 22–23% of all the fresh surface water on Earth. The secret is depth: it fills a crack in the continent, a rift where the crust is pulling apart by about 4 mm a year, making it **deeper than any other lake**. At 25 to 30 million years old it is also the oldest, and its isolation has produced thousands of species, many found nowhere else, including the Baikal seal.

slides.question: How deep is Lake Baikal at its deepest point?
slides.explanation: 1,642 metres, the deepest of any lake. The rift beneath it keeps deepening the basin.

slides.label: maximum depth of Lake Baikal, the deepest lake on Earth
slides.text: In winter the water can be clear enough to see 30 to 40 metres down.

slides.question: Baikal is only 79 km across at its widest. How long is it?
slides.explanation: 636 km, nearly as long as Lake Tanganyika (673 km), the world’s longest freshwater lake. Both are long and thin because they fill rift valleys where the crust is pulling apart.

slides.heading: Baikal in numbers
items: About 23,600 km³ of water, 22–23% of fresh surface water
25–30 million years old, the world’s oldest lake
The rift widens by about 4 mm a year

slides.heading: Baikal holds more water than all five Great Lakes together
slides.note: Volumes in cubic kilometres; the Great Lakes figure is their combined total.

slides.heading: A lake in a crack
slides.text: Baikal sits in the Baikal Rift Zone, where the Earth’s crust is slowly tearing apart. The rift keeps deepening the basin, which is why the lake has lasted tens of millions of years instead of filling with sediment. Its waters hold more than 1,000 species of plants and 2,500 of animals, many of them endemic.
